title: Si + Imperfect Subjunctive: Imagining Each Option

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know the imagined *si* from B1 Unit 4: *si* + the imperfect subjunctive, with the conditional in the result (*Si yo fuera tú, hablaría con el profesor*). It is the natural way to describe what each status option would mean, because each one is a situation that does not exist yet. The sentences here describe the options without taking sides.

sections.title: One option, one imagined result
rows: Si Puerto Rico fuera un estado, sus ciudadanos elegirían senadores con voto.
Si fuera independiente, tendría su propia política exterior.
Si eligiera la libre asociación, firmaría un acuerdo con Estados Unidos.

items.spanish: Si Puerto Rico fuera un estado, tendría dos senadores en el Congreso.
items.english: If Puerto Rico were a state, it would have two senators in Congress.

items.spanish: Si la isla fuera independiente, tendría su propia política exterior.
items.english: If the island were independent, it would have its own foreign policy.

items.spanish: Si los resultados fueran vinculantes, el Congreso tendría que respetarlos.
items.english: If the results were binding, Congress would have to respect them.

items.spanish: Si eligieran la libre asociación, firmarían un acuerdo con Estados Unidos.
items.english: If they chose free association, they would sign an agreement with the United States.

sections.content: Never put the conditional after *si*: say *si fuera*, not *si sería*. The *-ra* and *-se* forms are the same (*fuera* and *fuese*). Say each option the same way, with a *si* clause and a result, and the sentence describes it without judging it.
